newsitem.title: Italy: FOCUS-Striking Italian airport workers cause chaos.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Striking Italian airport workers cause chaos.

text.p: Thousands of striking airport workers caused chaos across Italy on Tuesday, with Milan's Linate airport closed for several hours as demonstrators protested on the runways.
State carrier Alitalia cancelled 143 national and international flights ahead of the one-day strike by staff demanding higher pay.
The airline said that of 136 flights normally scheduled between 1000 and 1300 local time, 93 had gone ahead.

It said that was seven fewer than planned but blamed demonstrations at Linate, where some 300 ground staff occupied the runways. Some flights bound for the airport were diverted to other airports, such as Genoa and Trieste.
Passengers arriving at Rome's Fiumicino airport had to wait an average of two hours for their luggage as several major airlines resorted to using their own staff to unload planes.
"I've been waiting more than two hours for my cases. It's a national disgrace," said Italian Paolo Ferrari, 25, returning to Rome from a trip to New York.
All departures were delayed and some, including international flights, were cancelled from the Italian capital.
A small group of demonstrators in vehicles at Fiumicino tried to prevent a British Airways flight to London from leaving its bay but police kept them away.
Some 15,000 ground employees are seeking more pay. Trades unions called the strike to try to force the government to renegotiate old pay contracts, which expired in June 1995.

Alitalia, repeatedly hit by strikes of its own staff during the past year, took out full-page advertisements in Italian newspapers on Tuesday promising to do everything possible to minimise the impact on passengers.
Bus, tram and commuter train workers are due to strike across much of Italy for eight hours on Wednesday.

In Rome, the strike was postponed to next Tuesday after a plea from mayor Francesco Rutelli for it not to coincide with a visit by International Olympic Committee officials looking at Rome's bid to host the 2004 Summer Games. The IOC visit starts on Wednesday.
"If the strike had gone ahead as planned the city would have presented a chaotic, inadequate image, out of keeping with its daily reality," newspapers quoted Rutelli as saying.
